sentences.text: The name Erectopus translates to "upright foot".
Estimates of its size vary, with one study suggesting a weight of 200 kg and another proposing it reached 5 meters in length and weighed 315 kg.
The holotype specimen was discovered in the early 1870s in phosphate-bearing beds at Louppy-le-Château in eastern France.
Charles Barrois first described the initial fossils, consisting of two teeth and a vertebra, in 1875.
Henri-Émile Sauvage established the species Megalosaurus superbus in 1882 based on these remains, but Friedrich von Huene created the genus Erectopus and named the species Erectopus superbus in 1923.
In 1932, von Huene proposed a second species, Erectopus sauvagei, believing the original Barrois fossils belonged to a different species.
The recovered maxilla serves as the lectotype, while the casts of the original Pierson specimen serve as the plastotype.
Allain (2005) classified Erectopus superbus within the Allosauroidea, a group equivalent to Carnosauria.
The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Erectopus as Metriacanthosauridae.
Fossils of Erectopus have been found in the Lower Cretaceous La Penthiève Beds Formation of France and possibly the Cernavodă Formation of Romania.
Erectopus lived during the Barremian to Cenomanian stages, between 125.77 and 93.9 million years ago.
